# Goals of This Section

## Goals of This Section

Today we will:

- Discuss trends in educational attainment in Canada
- Introduce Human Capital Theory of education investment
- Introduce the Signalling Model of education investment
- Discuss empirical methods to estimate returns to schooling
- Review empirical evidence on returns to schooling
- Discuss job training

# Human Capital Theory

## Human Capital Theory

- Firms often invest in [physical capital]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} (e.g., machines, tools, buildings)
  - Incur some cost today to invest in capital
  - Boosts the productive ability of workers
  - Increases the output flow in the future
- Decision to invest is made by comparing costs to benefits
  - Invest if benefits outweigh costs
  - Costs are usually upfront, while benefits occur slowly over time

## Human Capital Theory

::: {.callout-important}
## Human Capital
[Human Capital:]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} an individual's stock of productive skills, knowledge, and abilities

- People incur upfront costs for education, training, etc.
- Training improves productivity, and therefore income
- Individuals earn higher income streams in the future
:::

We study investments in human capital in a similar way to physical capital

## Human Capital Theory

Human capital investments involve some special considerations:

[Non-wage benefits:]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}

- Consumption value of education
- Differences in risk of unemployment in downturns

[Financing:]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}

- More difficult to finance education investments — no collateral

[Social versus private costs/benefits:]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}

- Private costs and benefits are specific to the individual
- But there may be social costs and benefits as well (e.g., positive externalities from education)

# Private Investments In Education

## Introduction

- The human capital investment decision boils down to comparing [lifetime income streams]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}
  - Different streams of income are associated with different levels of schooling
  - Higher levels of schooling usually lead to higher income streams
- We will outline a process to decide which stream to choose

To make the model tractable, we assume:

1. No direct utility or disutility from schooling
2. Hours of work are held fixed
3. Certainty of income streams
4. Individuals can borrow and lend at interest rate $r$

## Attending University

- Suppose we want to analyze whether it is financially worthwhile to attend university
  - Start from the perspective of an 18-year-old high school graduate
  - This student is deciding whether or not to attend university
  - Students who do not attend university move immediately into the workforce
- The graph on next slide depicts two income streams:
  - [Black line:]{.fg style="color: #555;"} university path
  - [Blue line:]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} high school path
  - [Red and yellow:]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} costs of attending university
  - [Green:]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"} benefits of university education

## Attending University

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {layout="[[-1], [1], [-1]]"}
![](images/clipboard-3559324769.png)
:::
::::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- [Direct costs]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} are in red: books, fees, tuition
- [Foregone wages]{.fg style="color: #f0ad4e;"} are in yellow: income not earned during university
- [Net wage gains]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"} are in green: earnings of university grad above high school grad

Beneficial to attend if [present value of green]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"} exceeds present value of yellow plus red
:::
::::::

## Attending University

- People will choose the level of schooling that maximizes the [net present value of lifetime earnings]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}
- Express the present value of earnings for a high school graduate as:

$$PV = \frac{Y}{(1+r)^0} + \frac{Y}{(1+r)^1} + \ldots + \frac{Y}{(1+r)^{T-18}}$$

Where:

- $Y$ = annual earnings of high school graduate
- $r$ = interest rate
- $T$ = expected retirement age

## Attending University

We can approximate the present value of earnings for a high school graduate as:

$$PV \approx Y + \frac{Y}{r} $$

(Approximation works if $T$ is long enough)

Now consider a person who attends [one year of university]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}:

- Incurs direct costs $D$ in the first year and earns no income in that year
- Every year they work, they gain an amount $\Delta Y$ above the high school graduate

## Attending University

Their income stream is:

$$PV^* = \frac{-D}{(1+r)^0} + \frac{Y + \Delta Y}{(1+r)^1} + \ldots + \frac{Y + \Delta Y}{(1+r)^{T-18}}$$

Which can be approximated as:

$$PV^* \approx -D + \frac{Y + \Delta Y}{r} $$

The [net present value]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} of attending this additional year of university is:

$$NPV = PV^* - PV \approx -(D + Y) + \frac{\Delta Y}{r} $$

## Attending University

::: {.callout-tip}
## Investment Condition

Attending university for one year is worthwhile if:

$$NPV > 0 \implies \frac{\Delta Y}{r} > D + Y $$

A person will continue attending more years of schooling until $MB = MC$:

$$ \frac{\Delta Y}{r} = D + Y $$
:::

## Attending University

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {layout="[[-1], [1], [-1]]"}
![](images/clipboard-18368519.png)
:::
::::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- [Marginal benefit curve]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"} is downward sloping
  - Each additional year of schooling yields a smaller increase in wages
- [Marginal cost curve]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} is upward sloping
  - Each additional year of schooling incurs higher direct costs, foregone wages, psychic costs
- [Optimum is where MB = MC]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}
:::
::::::

## Attending University

Another way to look at the schooling decision: the [internal rate of return (IRR)]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}

- The IRR is the interest rate that makes the NPV of an investment equal to zero
- In our setup, the IRR satisfies:

$$ 0 = -(D + Y) + \frac{\Delta Y}{IRR} $$

Rearranging gives:

$$ IRR = \frac{\Delta Y}{D + Y} $$

The IRR is the [percentage return]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} on the investment in schooling

## Attending University

- The alternative to attending university is to invest $D + Y$ at market interest rate $r$
  - Opportunity cost of investing in schooling is $r$
- If the [IRR exceeds $r$]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"}, then investing in schooling is worthwhile
- A person would continue to attend more years of schooling until:

$$ IRR = r \implies \frac{\Delta Y}{D + Y} = r $$

## Attending University

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {layout="[[-1], [1], [-1]]"}
![](images/clipboard-1015808942.png)
:::
::::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- Market interest rate is $r$ (horizontal line)
- [Internal rate of return IRR]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"} is decreasing in schooling
  - Each additional year of schooling yields a smaller wage increase
- [Optimum is where IRR = r]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}
- Yields same optimal schooling level as the MB = MC method
:::
::::::

## Comparative Statics

We can use this framework to analyze how policy and parameter changes affect schooling decisions:

- [Decrease in direct costs $D$]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"} (e.g., government introduces tuition subsidies)
  - Decreases marginal cost of schooling → [increases optimal schooling]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"}
- [Decrease in market interest rate $r$]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"} (e.g., due to monetary policy)
  - Increases present value of future earnings → [increases optimal schooling]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"}

## Comparative Statics

- [More progressive income tax]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} (higher taxes on high earners)
  - Decreases after-tax earnings gain $\Delta Y$ → [decreases optimal schooling]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}
- [Increase in pay for high school jobs]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} (e.g., oil sector boom)
  - Increases earnings of high school graduates $Y$
  - Raises the opportunity cost of attending school → [decreases optimal schooling]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}

## Complications

[Information asymmetries:]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}

- Students may not know the true costs and benefits of schooling
- May lead to under- or over-investment

[Disutility of schooling:]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}

- Students may dislike attending school — adds to marginal cost

[Different degrees have different returns:]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}

- Some fields lead to higher earnings than others
- Students must choose not only how much schooling, but what type

## Complications

::: {.callout-warning}
## Credit Constraints
A major complication is [financing]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}:

- Many students cannot afford the upfront costs of schooling
- May not be able to borrow against future earnings
- Leads to [under-investment in schooling]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} compared to the optimal level
:::

# Signalling

## Introduction

::: {.callout-note}
## Human Capital vs. Signalling
Two competing explanations for why education raises wages:

- [Human Capital model:]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"} education increases productivity; employers pay accordingly
- [Signalling model:]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} education reveals (rather than creates) productivity — it acts as a signal of worker ability
:::

Key assumptions of the **signalling model**:

- Education may not increase productivity
- Instead, it reveals productivity to employers
- People invest in education only to signal their ability to employers

## Model

The basics of the model:

- Employers [do not observe productivity]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} until after a worker is hired
- Employees know their own ability but find it difficult to credibly reveal it to employers
- Without knowing productivity, firms pay employees according to [average productivity]{.fg style="color: #555;"} in the population
- Under certain conditions, obtaining education can serve as a [signal of productivity]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}, allowing workers to be paid accordingly

## Model

::: {.callout-important}
## When Does Education Signal Ability?
For education to be informative about ability:

- It must be [costly to acquire]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}
- It must be [sufficiently more costly]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} for low-ability individuals than for high-ability individuals
  - Otherwise, low-ability workers might find it profitable to *fake* high ability
- [Employers' beliefs must be confirmed]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} in the future — otherwise, they will update their wage offers
:::

Given the conditions above, education helps solve an information problem — it correctly reveals ability through educational attainment, and workers are paid according to their true productivity

## Model

Assume that:

- There are two types of workers: [low ability (L)]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} and [high ability (H)]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"}
- A fraction $q$ are Type L, and $(1 - q)$ are Type H

[Type L workers:]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}

- Cost of education: $c_L(s) = s$
- Marginal Product (MP): $1$

[Type H workers:]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"}

- Cost of education: $c_H(s) = \frac{s}{2}$
- Marginal Product (MP): $2$

## Model

- Employees know their own ability, but employers do not
- Employers form *beliefs* about employee ability based on observed education levels
- If there were [no way to signal ability]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}, firms would offer everyone the same wage
  - The wage equals the [average productivity]{.fg style="color: #555;"}:

$$\bar{w} = 1 \cdot q + 2 \cdot (1 - q) = 2 - q$$

## Model

Example: 50% Low-Ability Workers ($q = 0.5$):

$$\bar{w} = 2 - q = 1.5$$

Recall that:

- Type L workers produce $MP = 1$
- Type H workers produce $MP = 2$

Therefore:

- [Type L is paid **more** than they produce]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"}
- [Type H is paid **less** than they produce]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}
- On average, total pay equals total production

## Model

Suppose employers observe education and form beliefs about how it relates to ability. One possible set of employer beliefs:

- Workers with education $s > s^*$ are [Type H]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"}
- Workers with education $s \le s^*$ are [Type L]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}
- $s^*$ is some cutoff level of education

Firms pay wages according to the believed type:

$$w =
\begin{cases}
2, & \text{if } s > s^* \\
1, & \text{if } s \le s^*
\end{cases}$$

## Model

Workers decide how much education to acquire. A worker of type $t$ maximizes utility:

$$U_t(s) = w(s) - c_t(s)$$

- All workers can obtain $U_t(s) = 1$ by acquiring **no education**
  - Therefore, the payoff to acquiring any education must satisfy $U_t(s) \ge 1$
- Workers will never find it useful to obtain **more than** $s^*$ years of education
  - Doing so increases costs without increasing payoffs
- Thus, the decision is binary: either **0** or $s^*$ years of education

## Model

[Type H Workers:]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"}

$$U_H(0) = w(0) - c_H(0) = 1 - 0 = 1$$

$$U_H(s^*) = w(s^*) - c_H(s^*) = 2 - \frac{s^*}{2}$$

A Type H worker will acquire $s^*$ years of education if $U_H(s^*) > U_H(0)$:

$$2 - \frac{s^*}{2} > 1 \implies s^* < 2$$

## Model

[Type L Workers:]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}

$$U_L(0) = w(0) - c_L(0) = 1 - 0 = 1$$

$$U_L(s^*) = w(s^*) - c_L(s^*) = 2 - s^*$$

A Type L worker will acquire $s^*$ years of education if $U_L(s^*) > U_L(0)$:

$$2 - s^* > 1 \implies s^* < 1$$

## Model

::: {.callout-tip}
## When Does Education Separate Types?

- If $s^* < 1$: both types acquire education $s^*$ — signal is [**not informative**]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}
- If $s^* > 2$: both types acquire **no education** — signal is [**not informative**]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}
- If $1 < s^* < 2$: Type H obtains $s^*$, Type L obtains none — education [**reveals worker type**]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"}
:::

## Model

[Equilibrium]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} occurs when $s^*$ lies **between 1 and 2**:

- This is an equilibrium because beliefs based on this strategy are **correct**
- A firm can only maintain beliefs if they are **validated** by observed behaviour
- Any $s^*$ between **1 and 2** will satisfy equilibrium conditions
  - The equilibrium with the **highest welfare** is the one closer to $s^* = 1$

[Separating equilibrium:]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"} different types choose different education levels

[Pooling equilibrium:]{.fg style="color: #555;"} everyone gets the same education level (no signalling occurs)

## Model

![](images/clipboard-3697593668.png)

## Model

Sometimes everyone is [worse off]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} under the separating equilibrium:

- Recall in the pooling equilibrium, nobody gets education — everyone is paid $\bar{w} = 2 - q$
- Under the separating equilibrium:
  - [Type L are paid $1$]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} — worse off unless $q = 1$
  - [Type H are paid $2 - \frac{s^*}{2}$]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} — worse off unless $s^* > 2q$
- In our previous example where $q = 0.5$: Type H individuals are worse off for any $s^* > 1$

## Model

::: {.callout-note}
## Key Ideas of the Signalling Model

- Depending on firm beliefs about the relationship between education and ability, it may be worthwhile to acquire education
- There must be a difference in the [cost of acquiring education]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} for high- and low-ability workers
- If firms' beliefs are not confirmed, they are not sustainable in equilibrium
:::

# Estimating Returns to Schooling

## Introduction

- We studied two theories of private education investment
  - These theories explain why individuals might invest in education
- Empirical economists estimate the size of the return using data
- We will study how empirical economists approach estimation
  - Mostly based on the [Human Capital Earnings Function]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}
- Results from existing research:
  - Rates of return to additional education are large
  - Some evidence they are rising over time
  - Returns are mostly attributed to human capital, but there is some evidence of signalling effects

## The Human Capital Earnings Function

::: {.callout-important}
## Mincer Equation
Most estimates of the return to education are based on the [Human Capital Earnings Function]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} (also known as the Mincer Equation):

$$\ln Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,schl + \beta_2\,exp + \beta_3\,exp^{2} + \epsilon$$

Where:

- $Y$ is some measure of earnings, income, or wages
- $schl$ is years of schooling
- $exp$ is potential experience: $exp = age - schl - 5$
:::

## The Human Capital Earnings Function

The Mincer equation uses the [natural logarithm of $Y$]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} as the dependent variable

When we use the natural log, coefficients measure the [percent change]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} in the dependent variable per unit change in the independent variable:

$$\beta_{1} = \frac{\partial \ln Y}{\partial schl} = \frac{\partial \ln Y}{\partial Y} \cdot \frac{\partial Y}{\partial schl} = \frac{1}{Y} \cdot \frac{\partial Y}{\partial schl}$$

::: {.callout-tip}
## Interpretation of $\beta_1$
$\beta_{1}$ is interpreted as the [internal rate of return (IRR)]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} — the percent change in yearly earnings per additional year of schooling
:::

## The Human Capital Earnings Function

One way to estimate this equation is to use [Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} regression

Two main data sources in Canada:

[Canadian Census:]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}

- Large sample sizes
- Detailed information on education and income
- Only conducted every 5 years

[Labour Force Survey (LFS):]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}

- Monthly survey
- Smaller sample sizes
- Less detailed information on education and income

## The Human Capital Earnings Function

```{r}
lfs <- read_csv("pub0925.csv") %>% clean_names() %>%
  mutate(educyrs = case_when(
    educ == 0 ~ 8,
    educ == 1 ~ 11,
    educ == 2 ~ 12,
    educ == 3 ~ 13,
    educ == 4 ~ 14,
    educ == 5 ~ 16,
    educ == 6 ~ 18,
    TRUE ~ NA_real_
  ),
  hrlyearn = hrlyearn/100) %>%
  filter(hrlyearn > 0) %>%
  mutate(
    educ_f = factor(
      educ,
      labels = c(
        "0–8 years",
        "Some high school",
        "High school graduate",
        "Some postsecondary",
        "Postsecondary certificate",
        "Bachelor's degree",
        "Graduate degree"
      )
    ),
    educ_f = relevel(educ_f, ref = "High school graduate")
  )




library(broom)

# Run the regression
mod <- lm(log(hrlyearn) ~ educyrs, data = lfs)

# Extract coefficients
b <- coef(mod)

# Build equation label
eq_label <- paste0(
  "ln(Y) = ",
  round(b[1], 3), " + ",
  round(b[2], 3), " * S"
)

ggplot(filter(lfs, age_12 == "05"), aes(x = educyrs, y = log(hrlyearn))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "blue", size = 1.2) +
  annotate("text",
           x = min(lfs$educyrs, na.rm = TRUE),
           y = max(log(lfs$hrlyearn), na.rm = TRUE),
           label = eq_label,
           hjust = 0, vjust = 1,
           size = 5
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Hourly Earnings by Years of Education for Canadians Aged 25 to 44",
    x = "Years of Education",
    y = "Log Hourly Earnings",
    caption = "Data Source: Statistics Canada Labour Force Survey"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12)
  )


```

## The Human Capital Earnings Function

- Graph above shows data on schooling and hourly earnings from the LFS in September 2025 (black dots) and the fitted OLS regression line (blue line)
- There is a clear [positive relationship]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"} between schooling and earnings

Issues with this graph:

- Does not control for experience
- Education data not actually stored in years of schooling
  - Actually stored in categories (e.g., high school graduate, some university, university degree)
  - Categories converted to approximate years

## The Human Capital Earnings Function

A more accurate approach:

- Run the [full Mincer equation regression]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}
  - Control for experience or age
- Use [categorical education variables]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} instead of years of schooling
  - Omit one group as the "reference category"
  - Coefficients measure the percent difference in earnings relative to the reference category
- Slide below shows results from a Mincer equation regression using September LFS data

## The Human Capital Earnings Function

```{r}
library(modelsummary)


mod_men <- lm(log(hrlyearn) ~ educ_f + factor(age_12), data = filter(lfs, gender== 1))
mod_women <- lm(log(hrlyearn) ~ educ_f + factor(age_12), data = filter(lfs, gender == 2))




modelsummary(
  list(
    "Men"   = mod_men,
    "Women" = mod_women
  ),
  estimate    = "{estimate} ({std.error})",
  statistic   = NULL,
  coef_omit   = "factor\\(age_12\\)|\\(Intercept\\)",
  coef_rename = function(x) gsub("^educ_f", "", x),
  gof_omit    = "IC|Log|Adj|AIC|BIC|F"
)

```

## Ability Bias

::: {.callout-important}
## Ability Bias
[Ability bias:]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} higher-ability people choose more schooling but would earn higher wages even without schooling

- OLS estimate reflects both the [return to schooling]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} and the [return to ability]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}
- Ability bias is thought to be [positive]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} → OLS [overestimates]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} the return to schooling
:::

## Ability Bias

Suppose the true earnings equation is:

$$\ln Y = \beta_{0} + \beta_1 schl + \beta_2 abil + \epsilon$$

Where $\epsilon$ has $E[\epsilon \mid schl, abil] = 0$

Assume schooling increases with ability:

$$abil = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 schl + v$$

with $v$ uncorrelated with $schl$

## Ability Bias

If we estimate a regression [omitting ability]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}:

$$\ln Y = \tilde{\beta}_1 schl + e$$

The OLS coefficient on schooling equals:

$$\tilde{\beta}_s = \frac{Cov(lnY, s)}{Var(s)}$$

## Ability Bias

Plug $\ln Y = \beta_1 schl + \beta_2 abil + \epsilon$ into the formula for $\tilde{\beta}_s$:

$$\tilde{\beta}_s = \frac{Cov(\beta_{0} + \beta_1 schl + \beta_2 abil + \epsilon, schl)}{Var(schl)}$$

Because $\beta_0$ is constant and $\epsilon$ is uncorrelated with $schl$:

$$\tilde{\beta}_s = \frac{\beta_1 Var(schl) + \beta_2 Cov(abil, schl)}{Var(schl)} = \beta_1 + \beta_2 \alpha_1$$

## Ability Bias

::: {.callout-tip}
## The Bias Formula

$$\tilde{\beta}_s = \underbrace{\beta_1}_{\text{true return}} + \underbrace{\beta_2 \alpha_1}_{\text{ability bias}}$$

The ability bias $\beta_2 \alpha_1$ depends on:

- $\beta_2$: the earnings return to ability
- $\alpha_1$: the relationship between ability and schooling

If both are positive → ability bias is positive → [OLS overestimates the return to schooling]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}
:::

## Addressing Ability Bias

Economists have developed methods to address ability bias:

[Twin Studies:]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}

- Compare earnings of identical twins with different schooling levels
- Presumably, twins have the same level of ability — comparing them avoids ability bias

[Instrumental Variables (IV):]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}

- Method that isolates variation in schooling unrelated to ability
- E.g., changes in compulsory schooling laws, proximity to university
- These changes affect schooling but are unrelated to ability

## Twin Studies

::: {.callout-note}
## Ashenfelter and Rouse (1998)
- Used data on identical twins in the US (collected at a Twins festival)
- [OLS estimate:]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} biased return of about **11%** per year
- [Twin differences estimate:]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"} return of about **7%** per year
- Suggests [ability bias of about 4 percentage points]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}
:::

## Compulsory Schooling

- Another method: use changes in [compulsory schooling laws]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} as an instrument for schooling
- Several US states have a minimum school leaving age (generally around 16 years old)
- Students born earlier in the year can leave school earlier
  - Someone born in January can leave earlier than someone born in December of the same year
  - On average, people born later in the year have more schooling
- [Angrist and Krueger (1991)]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} use this variation to estimate returns to schooling
  - Estimate a return of about **7–10%** per year of schooling

## Compulsory Schooling

- Canada has maximum school entry laws and minimum school leaving laws
  - Over time, students mandated to enter school earlier and leave later
  - This increases average schooling levels, [unrelated to ability]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"}
- [Oreopoulos (2006)]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} uses this variation to estimate returns to schooling in Canada
  - Finds that an additional year of compulsory schooling increases earnings by about **7–12%**

## Compulsory Schooling

![](images/schlaws_oreop.png){fig-align="center"}

## Signalling

- All studies cited so far have attributed returns to schooling to [human capital accumulation]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}
- Some studies have attempted to separate human capital from signalling effects
- [Ferrer and Riddell (2002)]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} use Canadian data to estimate credential effects
  - Look at people with same years of schooling, but different credentials
  - E.g., someone with a high school diploma versus someone with the same years but did not graduate
- [Find that obtaining the credential does matter]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"} — consistent with some signalling

# Social Returns to Education

## Social Returns to Education

- Most discussion so far has focused on [private returns]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} to education (returns to the individual)
- We know there are [positive externalities]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"} to society as a whole:
  - States/provinces with higher average education have higher earnings in excess of the private return
  - More highly educated immigrants in STEM have a positive effect on productivity of other workers
  - More highly educated populations have [lower crime rates]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"}, [better health outcomes]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"}, [more civic participation]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"}

::: {.callout-tip}
## Policy Implication
Because social returns exceed private returns, there is a rationale for [public subsidies to education]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}
:::

# Education and Inequality

## Education and Inequality

- Earnings inequality has increased in many countries over the past few decades
- In Canada:
  - Rose over the 80s and 90s
  - Has been stable since

Two sources of rising inequality:

- [Returns to schooling]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}: college premium has grown
- [Inequality within education groups]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}: growing wage dispersion even among equally-educated workers

In Canada, much of the rise is related to [inequality within education groups]{.fg style="color: #555;"}

## Education and Inequality

## Education and Inequality

![](images/ineq2.png){fig-align="center"}

## Education and Inequality

Why has the return to education increased?

[Skill-Biased Technological Change:]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}

- New technologies increase demand for skilled workers
- Increases the wage premium for higher education
- Thought to be the major driver in the 1980s

[Globalization:]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}

- Increased trade and outsourcing
- Reduces demand for lower-skilled workers locally

[Institutional Changes:]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}

- Decline in unionization, changes in labour market policies
- Negatively affects bargaining power of lower-skilled workers

# Training

## Introduction

- Formal schooling is one way to develop human capital
- Another important way is through [job training]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}

::: {.callout-important}
## Types of Training
- [General Training:]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"} skills that are useful at many firms
- [Specific Training:]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} skills that are only useful at a specific firm
:::

Training helps develop skills that increase human capital — in this section we evaluate the economics of job training

## Who Pays for Job Training

- It is not uncommon for firms to pay for job training
  - Some companies provide training to all employees
  - Others fund things like MBA programs
- Under what circumstances would the firm pay versus the individual?
- The answer [differs for general versus specific training]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}

## Who Pays for Job Training

[General training:]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"} employees fund training themselves

- General training increases productivity at [many firms]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"}
  - Employees can take skills to other firms
- Firms offer higher wages to employees with general training (very similar to schooling)
- But [employees fund the training themselves]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}
  - Pay for it as long as lifetime wage increase exceeds the cost of training

## Who Pays for Job Training

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {layout="[[-1], [1], [-1]]"}
![](images/costsbenefitstrain.png){fig-align="center"}
:::
::::

::: {.column width="50%"}
[General training illustrated:]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}

- Without training: employee earns wage $W_a$ (equals VMP without training)
- Employee who gets training:
  - Earns lower wage $VMP_t$ [during training]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}
  - Earns higher wage $VMP^*$ [after training]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"}
- Worth it for employee if present value of wage increase exceeds cost of training
:::
::::::

## Who Pays for Job Training

[Specific training:]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} firms pay

- Specific training only increases productivity [at one firm]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}
  - Skills not transferable to other firms
- [Company would pay]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"} if benefits exceed costs
  - Benefits: higher productivity of employee
  - Costs: wages paid during training period
- Would not have to pay higher wages — there is [no competition]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"} for workers with this specific skill

## Who Pays for Job Training

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {layout="[[-1], [1], [-1]]"}
![](images/costsbenefitstrain.png){fig-align="center"}
:::
::::

::: {.column width="50%"}
[Specific training illustrated:]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}

- Before and after training: employee earns wage $W_a$
- [Firm costs]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} during training: $W_a - VMP_t$
- [Firm benefits]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"} after training: $VMP^* - W_a$
- Worth it if present value of benefits exceeds present value of costs
:::
::::::

## Who Pays for Job Training

[Shared investment]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} — happens when there is a risk of the individual leaving after training:

- Firms pay below $W_a$ during the training period (but still above the VMP during training)
- Pay above $W_a$ after training (but below the employee's VMP)
- In this way, employee and employer [share the costs and benefits]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}

## Who Pays for Job Training

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {layout="[[-1], [1], [-1]]"}
![](images/specifictrain.png){fig-align="center"}
:::
::::

::: {.column width="50%"}
[Shared specific training:]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}

During training period:

- [Employee cost:]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} earning less than $W_a$
- [Employer cost:]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} paying above VMP

After training period:

- [Employee benefit:]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"} earning more than $W_a$
- [Employer benefit:]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"} paying below VMP
:::
::::::

## Who Pays for Job Training

- For illustrative purposes, we have depicted training as a one-time event
  - In reality, training is often ongoing throughout a worker's career
  - Workers may receive multiple types of training at different times
  - Firms may have formal training programs or informal on-the-job training
- A more gradual training leads to smoother curves — but the lesson is still the same

## Who Pays for Job Training

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {layout="[[-1], [1], [-1]]"}
![](images/earngrowth.png){fig-align="center"}
:::
::::

::: {.column width="50%"}
[Gradual shared training:]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}

- Lesson is still the same
- [Costs gradually fall]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} over time during training
- [Benefits gradually grow]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"}
- Worth it for employer and employee if benefits exceed costs
:::
::::::

## Training and Government

Governments often subsidize job training programs. Several rationales for public funding:

- [Positive externalities]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} from a more productive workforce
- Individuals may [underinvest due to credit constraints]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}
- [Imperfect information]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} about training benefits

Some current government funding initiatives:

- [Canada-Ontario Job Grant]{.fg style="color: #555;"}: funds businesses to train employees
- [NPower Canada:]{.fg style="color: #555;"} registered charity providing tech training, funded by government

## Training and Government

- An active area of labour economics is [program evaluation]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} — evaluating the effectiveness of government training programs
- In some cases, people are [randomly allocated]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"} to training programs
  - Can directly compare outcomes of those who received training to those who did not
  - Identifies the causal effect of training
- In most cases, people [self-select]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} into training programs
  - People in training and comparison groups differ in many ways besides training
  - Makes it difficult to isolate the effect of training itself

## Training and Government

Program evaluation uses econometric techniques to address selection issues:

- [Difference-in-Differences (DiD):]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} compare changes in outcomes over time between treatment and control groups
- [Propensity Score Matching (PSM):]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} match individuals in treatment and control groups based on observable characteristics
- [Instrumental Variables (IV):]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} use external factors that affect training participation but not outcomes directly

::: {.callout-note}
## Evidence from Program Evaluation
- U.S. training programs have [positive results]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"} for young women from poorer backgrounds
- But [no effect for men]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}
- More successful programs emphasize [human capital investment]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} over job search assistance
:::

# Summary

## Summary

- [Education is an investment in human capital]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} — increases productivity and earnings potential
- The [Human Capital model]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"} explains schooling decisions based on costs and benefits
  - People invest in schooling until marginal benefit equals marginal cost
- The [Signalling model]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} emphasizes education as a signal of ability
  - Education reveals productivity to employers rather than creating it

## Summary

- Empirical estimates of [returns to schooling are around 7–10% per year]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}
  - Ability bias may lead to overestimation; twin and IV studies correct for this
- [Job training]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} is another important way to develop human capital
  - General training funded by workers; specific training funded by firms; often shared
